steps.title: Kickoff!
steps.body: A kickoff starts each half of the game. One team kicks the ball far down the field, and the other team catches it and runs it back.

steps.title: After a score
steps.body: Kickoffs also happen after a touchdown or a field goal. The team that just scored kicks the ball to the other team.

steps.title: The returner
steps.body: The player who catches the kick is the kick returner. Their job is to run the ball back as far as they can.

choices: At the start of each half
steps.explanation: Kickoffs start each half, and they come after touchdowns and field goals too.

steps.statement: After a team scores a touchdown, that team kicks off to the other team.
steps.explanation: Yes! The scoring team kicks, so the other team gets the ball.

steps.prompt: What does the kick returner try to do?
choices: Catch the kick and run it back
steps.explanation: The returner catches the ball and runs it back up the field.

steps.title: Touchback
steps.body: If the kick goes into the end zone and the returner stays there, it is a touchback. Play stops, and their team starts from a set spot on the field.

steps.statement: On a touchback, the receiving team gets the ball without running it out.
steps.explanation: Right. A touchback is a safe choice: no run, but a good starting spot.

steps.title: Onside kick
steps.body: Sometimes the kicking team wants the ball back. They kick it short on purpose and try to grab it. That is an onside kick.

steps.title: Ten yards
steps.body: The ball must go 10 yards before the kicking team can grab it. The other team can grab it any time.

steps.prompt: Why would a team try an onside kick?
steps.explanation: An onside kick is a way to try to keep the ball, usually when a team is behind late in the game.

steps.statement: On an onside kick, the kicking team can grab the ball after it goes 10 yards.
steps.explanation: Yes. Before 10 yards, only the other team may grab it.

steps.prompt: When do teams most often try onside kicks?
choices: When they are losing near the end
On the first kick of the game
steps.explanation: A team that is behind late needs the ball back, so the risk is worth it.

steps.statement: An onside kick is a long, high kick down the field.
steps.explanation: Not quite. An onside kick is short, so the kicking team has a chance to get it.

steps.title: Punt return
steps.body: When a team punts, a player on the other team catches it and tries to run it back. That is a punt return.

steps.title: Fair catch
steps.body: The returner can wave one arm over their head before catching. That is a fair catch: nobody may tackle them, but they can't run after catching.

steps.prompt: How does a returner ask for a fair catch?
choices: Waves one arm over their head
steps.explanation: Waving one arm over the head is the fair catch signal.

steps.statement: After a fair catch, the returner can run with the ball.
steps.explanation: Not quite. With a fair catch, play stops where they catch it. In exchange, nobody may hit them.

steps.prompt: Why call for a fair catch?
steps.explanation: Tacklers are running right at the returner. A fair catch keeps them safe.

steps.prompt: Match each kick to what it does.

pairs.right: Short kick to get the ball back

steps.explanation: Each kick has its own job. Kickoffs start play, punts give the ball away far from your goal, and field goals score.
